Herbert was held to 209 yards with a pick, and the exact OL/mobility issues the Skeptic flagged (Slater, Tuipulotu) showed up live — the reverse-line-movement trap flag called this correctly.

team_results.recap: Detroit led 21-0 before New Orleans — as the flagged depleted secondary and 49.5 total both foreshadowed — stormed back to tie it 24-24 late in regulation, forcing overtime. Jahmyr Gibbs (3 TD, 156 yards) and a Goff-to-St. Brown OT score pulled out a 31-30 win after New Orleans' 2-point try for the outright win failed. The Skeptic's secondary-depletion flag was directionally right even though DET escaped with the pick intact.

Dallas lost 28-20 at the Giants despite entering as road favorites; the Skeptic's rebuttal — that the rebuilt post-Parsons-trade defense was a real liability, not added strength — played out as New York piled up 394 total yards to Dallas's 244 and controlled the game with an 8-minute third-quarter drive.

Tennessee was outgained 361-195 and held to a garbage-time touchdown in a 23-10 loss to the Jets, whose defense limited Cam Ward to 140 yards passing and 68 rushing yards allowed. It's the Titans' sixth straight season-opening loss.

The Jets beat Tennessee 23-10, outgaining the Titans 361-195. QB Justin Fields/OC Frank Reich's offense scored on an opening 8-play drive and the defense limited Cam Ward to 140 yards passing behind a strong Aaron Glenn-coached unit in year two.

The Giants beat Dallas 28-20 on Sunday Night Football, John Harbaugh's debut win, behind Jaxson Dart (230 yards passing, 3 TD, 0 INT, plus 54 rushing yards) and a 394-244 total-yardage edge. Dart became the first QB in NFL history to open a season with 3 pass TD, 50+ rush yards, and a 130+ rating — the pregame 'unproven Dart/Skattebo combo' negative didn't hold up at all.

Arizona's stunning 26-14 win — Jacoby Brissett throwing for 277 yards/1 TD, Trey McBride going for 95 yards/1 TD, rookie HC Mike LaFleur winning his debut — was the NFL's biggest Week 1 upset, coming from the week's single lowest win probability on the board (14%).

Lost 9-3 in a rainy slugfest at Soldier Field. Minnesota's pass rush (Dallas Turner: 2 sacks, 10 pressures) smothered Caleb Williams, who then left in the 4th with a hamstring injury. Three CHI turnovers or special-teams failures (Murphy INT, forced Swift fumble, blocked FG) decided it. CHI's OL downgrade (RT Wright DNP) was a real, underweighted signal.
Won 9-3 at 35% despite the three confirmed absences that drove its number down. Defense and Aaron Jones (105 rush yds) were enough in a weather-suppressed game.

Trap flag false alarm. Drew Lock started for the injured Darnold and was nearly flawless (235 yds, 3 TD, all to Smith-Njigba, 9-155-3) in a 31-7 rout. It was Seattle's 10th straight win over Arizona. Cleveland won 23-19 in Tampa's home opener: the Browns were held without a TD on their first eight drives, then Deshaun Watson (24/30, 238 yds, 2 TD) led two second-half TD drives, the winner to Blake Whiteheart. After a 2+ hour weather delay with 2:00 left, CLE's defense stopped Tampa's go-ahead attempt. Mayfield was efficient (21/24) but the offense managed only 19 points. The 'depleted, QB-controversy CLE' case turned out to be mostly narrative, and TB's own weak Week 1 form was the better signal.

Road upset as a ~24% underdog. The QB-benching and fan-revolt storyline that dragged CLE's number down didn't show up on the field: Watson was sharp and the defense held a Bucs offense that was already struggling in Week 1.

Lost 26-14 at home to LV. Kirk Cousins threw 3 TDs and the Raiders forced three turnovers. The confirmed two-starter OL injury cluster the Skeptic flagged, which dropped LAC from 0.75 raw to 0.61, was validated. LAC is now 0-2.

QB drop-off meets an opponent built to exploit it (L6): Winston at 4.1 YPA in relief, a 40-mph-gust nor'easter capping the pass game, NYG's 5.6-YPC run defense vs. healthy TEN backs, Burns missing all practice, and ex-NYG coach Daboll as TEN's OC. The line already fell 3 points.

team_results.recap: KC won 24-10 at MIA, a sloppy grind rather than a blowout (Mahomes 20/24, 246, 2 TD, 1 INT; Walker 2 TD). MIA lost Achane on the opening drive, and KC didn't go up two scores until 2:55 left. The excluded favorite won, but the recommendation also won, so the policy cost nothing.

SF won 36-30 but ARI's Brissett went 38/52 for 280 yds and 2 TDs against the Bosa-less pass rush and pulled within one score late. Purdy (297 yds, 4 TD, incl. an 82-yd hook-and-ladder) and an onside-kick recovery sealed it. The Skeptic's DL-cluster concern was real: a 0.77 pick won by just 6. The pick was right, and the haircut was justified.

SEA lost 33-31 at WAS, snapping a 12-game win streak. Darnold was fine (379 yds, 4 TD) but threw 2 INTs, including a 50-yd pick-six by Kain Medrano with 3:57 left, and SEA lost the turnover battle 3-0. Backup QB Mariota threw 3 TDs against SEA's safety-less secondary: exactly the Skeptic's hard signal (both starting safeties out, 2nd straight East road trip). The Arbiter called the two sides even, and that was too generous.

Trap flag VALIDATED: CHI's third-string QB Case Keenum (Bagent wasn't cleared in time) threw for 247 yds and accounted for 3 TDs in a 27-7 Monday-night rout. PHI's depleted offense managed 248 yds, went 22% on third down and committed 3 turnovers. The L4/L5 framing held up exactly: the opponent-QB line move was priced in, and PHI's own form and injuries were the real story.

The nor'easter suppressed BOTH offenses (TEN nearly had no first down by halftime), so it neutralized TEN's ability to exploit the QB drop-off rather than amplifying it. The near-coin-flip 0.52 was well calibrated, even though the flag was wrong.

MIN won 15-10 on five Will Reichard field goals. It was the second time in three weeks without an offensive touchdown, and Murray leaned on Hockenson (13-119) with Jefferson out. The defense held winless MIA's Willis to 10 points. Exactly the Skeptic's script: a low-total grind with no cushion. The haircut below market (0.80 vs 0.83) was justified, and the pick still came through.

Upset: NE won 29-26 in Buffalo. Drake Maye overcame 2 turnovers with 3 TD passes, including a late go-ahead drive capped by a TD to Efton Chism, and S Craig Woodson intercepted Josh Allen on the final drive. NE's missing CB Gonzalez and DT Barmore didn't stop a competent starting QB from winning a division road game. The Skeptic's division-familiarity and Allen-knee notes were dismissed as soft and deserved more weight.

Trap flag was a FALSE ALARM, though a narrow one: KC won 30-27 at LV. LV led 13-10 at halftime, the teams combined for 34 fourth-quarter points, and Kenneth Walker III (177 rush yds, 2 TD) put KC ahead for good with 3:21 left. Cousins threw for 365. The flag correctly called a close peer game, but a 1-point reverse line move wasn't enough to predict a loss.

team_results.recap: JAX won 19-17 in London on Cam Little's 57-yard FG on the final play, after PHI went ahead 17-16 with 8 seconds left; Abdullah's 53-yard kickoff return set it up. Lawrence threw for 331 yds and 2 TDs vs a PHI team missing Barkley, D. Smith and much of its OL. The pick survived, but by the thinnest margin; the pregame worry that the line was public-inflated looked justified by how close it was.

The excluded largest favorite won easily, 26-3. Four Fairbairn FGs built a 12-3 half, then Stroud scored twice. Will Anderson had 3 sacks, and TEN managed only 187 yards (0-5). HOU's 0-4 own form (L5) didn't matter against a truly bad opponent. The policy cost nothing because JAX also won.

CIN led 28-10 before MIA added garbage-time points in a 31-24 final. The flag rested on 'questionable' tags that resolved in CIN's favor, plus a half-point move across 7.

team_results.recap: LA lost 37-34 in OT on MNF. Stafford threw for 383 yds and 3 TDs, but BUF ran for 234 (Allen 121) and Rousseau blocked an LA field goal in OT before Bass's winner. McVay blamed special teams. A 54.5-total shootout coin flip, as the board's variance note predicted.

ATL lost 30-23 in OT to a BAL team starting Tyler Huntley for an injured Lamar. Huntley threw 2 TDs with no INTs, tied it with ~40 seconds left plus a Henry 2-pt run, and scored the OT winner after Penix got hurt and Tua threw an INT to Hamilton. That makes another loss for the opponent-starting-QB-out profile (L7), now 1-3 since Week 3.

SEA lost 32-29 at home to a 5-0 SF team. Pineiro's go-ahead FG came with 1:09 left, then SF's defense got a turnover on downs. SEA's turnovers were costly. Better current form (SF +14.5 pd/g) beat the slim home-favorite tag.

CHI, a slight road favorite starting backup Tyson Bagent for Caleb Williams, was routed 31-7 at Lambeau. Bagent and then Keenum each threw 2 INTs, while Love threw for 367 yds. The 0.55 single-pass estimate didn't apply L10's 'favorite's OWN QB compromised' warning, and it should have.

flags: Favorite's own starting QB confirmed OUT + key-number move (L10/L13): Lamar OUT and C Jurgens OUT, so Huntley starts behind a backup center on the road in the division. The line fell from -4.5 to -3, landing on the key number, while CLE HC Monken (ex-BAL OC) knows Huntley's tendencies.

team_results.recap: The excluded largest favorite lost 18-16 to ARI on Chad Ryland's 43-yd FG at the gun, his 6th of the day. Stafford's TD to Parkinson with 47 seconds left wasn't enough. The Skeptic's kicking-crisis negative was exactly how it played out: LA settled for little in a game where ARI kicked six FGs. LA is 2-4 with 3 losses in 4 games despite the league-best yardage. The no-lazy-favorite policy saved a pick (KC won).

KC won 22-6 to move to 5-0. Kenneth Walker ran for 128 yds and 2 TDs, and Mahomes threw for 272 despite Rice and Thornton being out. Butker missed a PAT and a FG, which kept it from being a rout. LAC (0-6) managed 259 yards, and Herbert threw an INT; McConkey left with a concussion. The pick was never in danger.

IND (0.64) lost 26-20 at home to 0-5 TEN after leading 13-0 at the half. TEN won on special teams (58-yd punt return, blocked punt TD) and defense (6 sacks, 3 takeaways), while Ward threw for only 102 yds. This validates L5: IND's own form (-90.8 yds/g) was no better than TEN's, and the Arbiter's cut from 0.74 to 0.64 was still too generous.

JAX (used here, 0.52) lost 34-31 in London to HOU on a walk-off 49-yd Fairbairn FG after Cam Little's 60-yarder tied it. Stroud threw 3 TDs, and HOU has now won two straight after an 0-4 start. The Skeptic's case (HOU better than its record, JAX's LT out vs an elite rush, public-inflated price) was right to pull this to a near coin flip.

Trap flag validated. CLE won 13-10 on a walk-off 37-yd FG (after a BAL offside wiped out a block). Huntley went 19/31 for 165 and 'looked like a backup.' BAL led 10-0, then failed to score again, and a Derrick Henry fumble set up CLE's tying TD. Exactly the L13 profile: a road division favorite starting its own backup QB.
trap_flags: Favorite's own starting QB confirmed OUT + key-number move (L10/L13): Lamar OUT and C Jurgens OUT, so Huntley starts behind a backup center on the road in the division. The line fell from -4.5 to -3, landing on the key number, while CLE HC Monken (ex-BAL OC) knows Huntley's tendencies.

team_results.recap: TEN (0.36) won its first game, 26-20 at IND, rallying from 13-0 down with a punt-return set-up TD, a blocked-punt TD, 6 sacks and 3 takeaways. Robert Saleh's first win as TEN head coach.

ARI (0.19) won 18-16 at SoFi, a double-digit dog. The defense held a top LA passing offense in check after allowing 148 points in its prior four games, and Brissett threw for 218. Six FGs from Ryland, including the walk-off. New HC Mike LaFleur beat his former boss McVay.

lessons_learned.lesson: A trap flag backed by a concrete, quantifiable signal (reverse line movement plus a specific personnel weakness — LAC's OL/QB mobility issues) called the week's biggest upset correctly, while a trap flag built mainly on narrative (JAX's 'post-breakout letdown' and 'new DC is unknown' framing, with no concrete weakness identified) was a clean false alarm. Weight trap flags toward cases with at least one hard, checkable signal (line movement, a specific missing/injured starter) over pure storyline/vibes-based reasoning.

The no-lazy-favorite policy passed its first live test: the excluded largest Vegas favorite (LAC, 85% raw implied) suffered the week's biggest upset loss while the recommendation that went to the next-best team (DET) won, saving a pick outright. This is early evidence (n=1 week) that the policy's premise — the single largest raw-ML favorite is exactly where market/public overconfidence is most likely to get punished — has real teeth, not just theoretical justification. Continue applying it without softening.

The archived Week 1 board (data/history/week_analysis_2026_wk01.json) was missing entries for 4 of the week's 32 teams (SEA, NE, LA, SF — the SEA@NE and LA@SF games), even though every other game's both sides were represented. Future survivor-pick runs should verify all 32 teams for the week appear in the board before archiving/overwriting — a missing team can't be graded later and silently shrinks the calibration sample.

Apply L1's hard-signal-over-narrative rule to the OPPONENT's weaknesses too, not just to trap flags. Week 2's recommendation (TB, 0.76) lost to a CLE team whose low number rested mostly on narrative: fan revolt, QB-benching rumors, and a months-old Garrett trade that was already priced in. Meanwhile the teams discounted for confirmed, current multi-starter injury clusters (BAL, LAC) both lost. When a pick's case is mainly 'the opponent is a mess,' the Skeptic should require concrete, current evidence (injury report, efficiency data) of that mess. Otherwise the Arbiter should pull the number back toward the market or below it.

Teams pulled onto the shortlist only because of a large raw moneyline gap, despite weak own-team form, went 0-2 in Week 2 (TB -6.0 pd/g in Week 1, lost to CLE; LAC -12.0 pd/g, lost to LV). A team whose own recent point differential is poor should not jump straight to #1 recommendation on the matchup gap alone. Treat its weak own-form metrics as a real negative in the debate instead of explaining them away, and be especially wary when it is only a late addition to the shortlist.

Reverse line movement caused by a starting-QB injury is not a trap signal by itself. That news is already fully priced into the moved line, so it is not hidden sharp skepticism. SEA's flag (Darnold out, ~6-7 pt move) was a clean false alarm: backup Drew Lock beat a weak division rival 31-7 in Seattle's 10th straight win in the series. Flag QB-out spots only when the drop-off meets an opponent capable of exploiting it, and check the series/matchup history before calling a trap. BAL's validated flag, by contrast, rested on a broad multi-position injury cluster plus a hot opposing offense.

Favorites priced up mainly because the OPPONENT's starting QB is out went 1-2 in Week 3: PHI lost 27-7 to CHI's third-stringer Keenum, SEA lost 33-31 to WAS backup Mariota, and only SF beat Brissett. Add Week 2's TB loss to a 'mess' CLE team and the pattern holds. Experienced veteran backups (Keenum, Mariota, Brissett) playing at home are not a big drop-off. Once the market has moved the line for the QB news, don't stack a further discount on the opponent for it. Treat it as already priced, and grade the favorite on its OWN health and form. This extends L4/L6.

When the Skeptic's hard signal is a specific missing position group that lines up with what the opponent does well (SEA without both starting safeties vs. a WAS passing attack, on a 2nd straight East road trip), the Arbiter should not call it a wash just because the opponent's injury list is longer. Weigh injuries by matchup relevance, not by count: SEA at 0.72 lost, while the longer WAS injury list didn't matter. Similarly, SF's thinned pass rush let Brissett throw for 280 yds in a closer-than-expected game. The haircut on SF was correct, and a larger one on SEA was warranted.

Severe weather (heavy rain, ~40-mph gusts) suppresses BOTH offenses, so it compresses scoring and favors the side with the better defense and kicking. It does not specifically help an opponent exploit the favorite's backup QB. NYG's weather-amplified trap flag was a false alarm (won 12-7 on four FGs while TEN nearly had no first down by halftime). Don't count bad weather as a trap signal against a favorite unless the opponent's offense is clearly better suited to the conditions (e.g. a dominant run game vs. a run defense that is actually poor in current-season data).

Both Week 4 trap flags were false alarms that still ended as one-score games (KC won 30-27, GB won 17-14), bringing the season trap record to 3 validated vs 5 false alarms. A small reverse line move (KC -5.5 to -4.5, not crossing a key number) plus one personnel weakness identifies a CLOSE game, not a likely loss. Reserve the trap label for cases where the RLM is >=1.5 pts or crosses 3/7, or where the favorite's OWN starting QB/offense is compromised. A favorite facing an undrafted first-start rookie QB (GB vs Jalon Daniels) should rarely be flagged on its own form alone. Rookie-QB turnovers decided it.

Missing defensive starters on the underdog (NE without CB Gonzalez and DT Barmore) proved a weak positive against a healthy, competent starting QB in a division game: BUF (0.73) lost 29-26 to Drake Maye's 3 TDs. By contrast, the favorites facing backup/rookie QBs this week (GB, MIN, BAL after Lamar left) won ugly but won. When the opponent's starting QB is healthy and competent, count its defensive injuries as a modest edge only. Give division familiarity in a big-spread (>=7) home game a real haircut (~2-3 pts), not a 'soft' dismissal.

CIN's Week 5 trap flag was another false alarm (season trap record now 3 validated, 6 false alarms). It rested on two WRs listed 'questionable', not OUT, plus a half-point line move across 7. Chase was cleared that morning and scored, and CIN won by a TD after leading 28-10. A flag built on the favorite's own offense being compromised (L10) needs CONFIRMED absences: OUT/doubtful status, or the inactives list. Unresolved questionable tags do not qualify. If the status is still unresolved at run time, note the risk as a negative and haircut the number, but don't trap-flag it.

Backup-QB spots went against the favorite from BOTH directions in Week 5. ATL (0.57), favored because BAL's Lamar was out, lost to Huntley in OT, so the L7 'opponent QB out' profile is now 1-3 since Week 3. CHI (0.55), a road favorite starting its OWN backup (Bagent) in a division game at Lambeau, lost 31-7 on four INTs. Asymmetry: don't add any edge for the opponent's backup beyond the moved line (L7). A favorite starting its own backup QB on the road, especially in a division game, should be graded below 0.50 regardless of the moneyline. Apply this in the single-pass tier too, not just on the shortlist.

The no-lazy-favorite policy saved its 2nd pick of the season. LA (85% raw, Arbiter 0.81) lost 18-16 to 10-point dog ARI, while KC won. Season record: 3 no-cost, 1 cost-a-pick, 2 saved. The mechanism was one the Skeptic named: a confirmed broken phase (LA's kicking, 5/9 FG with the kicker released) on a team whose wins weren't matching its yardage (2-4 despite the league's best yds/g). When a big favorite has a dysfunctional unit that directly converts yards to points (kicking or red zone) AND a W-L record that trails its efficiency, haircut it harder than ~4 pts. Keep applying the exclusion without softening.

The tightened trap criteria (L10/L12/L13) went 1-for-1 in Week 6. BAL, the only flag, was a road division favorite with its OWN starting QB and starting C confirmed OUT, plus a line move from -4.5 to -3 onto the key number, and it lost 13-10. This contrasts with 0-for-3 on looser flags in Weeks 4-5 (season now 4 validated / 6 false alarms). Use 'favorite's own QB confirmed out + line moving against it onto/through a key number' as the template for the scarce trap label.

L5 validated again. IND, favored at -7 but with own-form yards differential (-90.8/g) no better than its opponent's, lost outright to 0-5 TEN even after the Arbiter cut it from 0.74 to 0.64. When a favorite's own yards differential is negative and no better than the opponent's, cap its probability near 0.55-0.58 regardless of the spread. The market is pricing the opponent's record, not the favorite's quality.
